cse-2023-ga-1.approach: Decide the part of speech first (the blank modifies the verb *missed*, so it must be an adverb), then pick the adverb whose meaning fits an all-or-nothing event like missing a train.

steps.title: The blank needs an adverb
steps.body: In "and _______ missed the train" the blank sits right before the verb **missed** and modifies it, so it must be an **adverb**. *Near* is mainly an adjective or preposition ("the near side", "near the station"); "near missed" is ungrammatical. That leaves *nearly*, *utterly* and *mostly*.

steps.title: Missing a train is all-or-nothing
steps.body: You either miss a train or you catch it — it cannot be done "partly". So adverbs that grade **how much** (*mostly* = for the most part) or **intensify** (*utterly* = completely) do not collocate with *missed the train*. *Nearly* means **almost**: the event very nearly happened but did not.

steps.title: Read the completed sentence
steps.body: "We reached the station late, and **nearly** missed the train." Arriving late explains why missing the train *almost* happened — the sentence is grammatical and logical.

optionAnalysis.reason: *Near* is an adjective/preposition; it cannot modify the verb *missed* ("near missed" is ungrammatical).
*Nearly* = almost: being late made missing the train almost happen.
*Utterly* is an intensifier for gradable states ("utterly exhausted"); missing a train cannot be done to a degree.
*Mostly* means "for the most part" — a train cannot be mostly missed.

cse-2023-ga-1.shortcut: Before the verb → adverb; with an either/or event the only sensible adverb is "nearly/almost".
pitfalls: Choosing *utterly* because it "sounds strong" — intensifiers need a gradable word to intensify.
cse-2023-ga-1.verification: Substitute each option: only "nearly missed the train" is both grammatical and meaningful.

cse-2023-ga-2.approach: Name the relation in the complete pair (*often* : *frequently* are synonyms), then test which option is a synonym of *kind*. *Kind* has two senses, which is why the official key gave marks to all.
concepts: Words with two parts of speech

steps.title: The relation is "same meaning"
steps.body: *Often* and *frequently* are both adverbs meaning "many times": the pair is a **synonym** pair. The instruction "(By word meaning)" confirms it — we need a word that **means the same as** *kind*.

steps.title: Kind as an adjective
steps.body: *Kind* (adj.) = gentle, benevolent. *Mean* and *cruel* are its **antonyms**, so (A) and (C) are out. *Kindly* (adj.: "a kindly old man") means the same as *kind* — a synonym under this reading.

steps.title: Kind as a noun
steps.body: *Kind* (n.) = sort, category: "a kind of fruit" = "a **type** of fruit". So *type* is an exact synonym under the noun reading — a different word, not just a derived form, exactly like *often*/*frequently*.

steps.title: Two defensible answers
steps.body: Both **Type** (noun sense) and **Kindly** (adjective sense) are synonyms of *kind*, and the question does not fix the part of speech. The official key therefore awarded **marks to all**. If one option must be chosen, *Type* is the cleaner analogue: a distinct word with the same meaning, whereas *kindly* is merely a derived form of *kind*.

answer.value: Official key: **marks to all** (ambiguous). Best single choice: **Type** — option (B)
answer.keyNote: The stored key is "MTA" (marks to all, official). It names no option letter, so no choice can match it; B (Type) is argued as the best answer and D (Kindly) is also defensible.

optionAnalysis.reason: *Mean* (unkind) is an **antonym** of *kind*, the opposite relation.
*Type* is a synonym of the noun *kind* ("a kind of" = "a type of") — a distinct word with the same meaning, like *often*/*frequently*.
*Cruel* is an **antonym** of *kind*.
Defensible but weaker: *kindly* (adj.) does mean *kind*, but it is only a derived form of the same word — this second valid reading is why marks were given to all.

pitfalls: Reading *kind* only as an adjective and rejecting *type* as unrelated.
Choosing an antonym (*mean*, *cruel*) — the given pair is a synonym pair.
cse-2023-ga-2.verification: Plug each into a sentence: "a kind of tree" = "a type of tree" ✓; "a kind man" = "a kindly man" ✓; "a kind man" ≠ "a mean/cruel man".

cse-2023-ga-3.approach: Run the recurrence **backwards**: $F_{n+1} = F_n + F_{n-1}$ gives $F_{n-1} = F_{n+1} - F_n$, so each earlier term is a subtraction of the two terms after it. Five subtractions reach $F_1$.
cse-2023-ga-3.given: $F_{n+1} = F_n + F_{n-1}$ for $n \ge 2$; $F_6 = 37$, $F_7 = 60$; all terms are natural numbers. Find $F_1$.

steps.title: Turn the recurrence around
steps.body:
From $F_{n+1} = F_n + F_{n-1}$:
$$F_{n-1} = F_{n+1} - F_n \qquad (n \ge 2)$$
The smallest allowed $n$ is $2$, which gives $F_1 = F_3 - F_2$ — so we can walk all the way down to $F_1$.

steps.title: Check forwards
steps.body: Starting from $4, 5$: $4+5 = 9$, $5+9 = 14$, $9+14 = 23$, $14+23 = 37$, $23+37 = 60$. Both given values are reproduced and every term is a natural number, so $F_1 = 4$.

optionAnalysis.reason: Backward subtraction gives $4, 5, 9, 14, 23, 37, 60$.
$5$ is $F_2$ — stopping one subtraction too early.
With $F_1 = 8$, $F_6 = 3F_1 + 5F_2 = 37$ forces $F_2 = \frac{13}{5}$, not a natural number.
$9$ is $F_3$ — stopping two subtractions too early.

cse-2023-ga-3.shortcut: Write terms in $a = F_1$, $b = F_2$: $F_6 = 3a + 5b$, $F_7 = 5a + 8b$ (Fibonacci coefficients). Then $8F_6 - 5F_7 = 24a - 25a = -a$, so $a = 5 \cdot 60 - 8 \cdot 37 = 300 - 296 = 4$.
pitfalls: Subtracting in the wrong order ($F_6 - F_7 = -23$) and getting negative terms.
Answering $F_2$ or $F_3$ by miscounting the indices — label each term as you go.

cse-2023-ga-4.approach: Convert "60% **of these** women" into a share of **all** pregnant women: $0.9 \times 0.6 = 0.54$. Then keep only the statement that follows from that number without assuming anything about how *often* care was received.
cse-2023-ga-4.given:
| Group | Share of the group above |
|---|---|
| Received care at least once | 90% of all pregnant women |
| — of them, from doctors | 60% |
| — of them, from other providers | 40% |

steps.title: Express everything as a share of all women
steps.body:
Doctor-care group: $90\% \times 60\% = 0.9 \times 0.6 = 0.54 = 54\%$ of all pregnant women.
Other providers: $0.9 \times 0.4 = 0.36 = 36\%$. No care at all: $100\% - 90\% = 10\%$. Check: $54 + 36 + 10 = 100$.

steps.title: Compare with one half
steps.body: Every woman in the 54% group received care from a doctor **at least once** (that is what the survey counted). Since $54\% > 50\%$, "more than half of the pregnant women received medical care at least once from a doctor" is **certain** — statement (A).

steps.title: Why the "at most once" options cannot be inferred
steps.body: The survey reports only **whether** care was received at least once, never **how many times**. A woman in the doctor group may have seen a doctor once or ten times, so nothing can be said with certainty about "at most once" — (C) and (D) are not inferable. (B) directly contradicts the 54%.

answer.value: **More than half received care at least once from a doctor** — option (A)

optionAnalysis.reason: $0.9 \times 0.6 = 54\% > 50\%$ of all pregnant women.
Contradicts the computed 54% — it comes from reading 60% as a share of *all* women and then misjudging, or from using 40%.
The data says nothing about the *number* of doctor visits, so "at most once" cannot be inferred with certainty.
Same flaw as (C): frequency of visits is unknown, so this is not certain either.

cse-2023-ga-4.shortcut: $0.6 \times 0.9$ is clearly above $0.5$ (since $0.6 \times 0.9 > 0.5 \iff 0.9 > 0.83$), so (A) holds; the "at most once" options are untestable.
pitfalls: Treating 60% as a share of *all* pregnant women instead of the 90% who received care.
Confusing "at least once" (given) with "at most once" (not given).
cse-2023-ga-4.verification: Even if the doctor and other-provider groups overlapped, at least $60\%$ of the $90\%$ saw a doctor, i.e. $\ge 54\%$ — still more than half.

cse-2023-ga-5.approach: Use one definition (a smooth surface has a tangent plane everywhere, so no edges or corners) and two quick examples — a sphere (convex everywhere) and a peanut shape (convex and concave) — to test each claim.

steps.title: Smooth means no edges and no corners
steps.body: A smooth surface bends gradually: at every point it has a well-defined tangent plane. An **edge** (like a cube's) or a **corner** (a vertex) is exactly where the surface is *not* smooth. So a smooth object can have neither — (D) is false.

steps.title: "Convex everywhere" is not forced
steps.body: A **peanut** (or a dumbbell, or a doughnut) is perfectly smooth, yet its "waist" curves *inwards* when seen from outside — concave there — while its ends bulge outwards. So the surface need not be convex everywhere: (B) is false.

steps.title: "Concave everywhere" is impossible
steps.body: Take the point of the object farthest from some interior point. Near it the whole object lies inside a sphere touching the surface there, so the surface bulges outwards (convex) at that point. A closed object therefore always has some convex region — (A) is false.

steps.title: What remains is a possibility statement
steps.body: (C) says the surface **may** be concave in some places and convex in others — true, as the peanut shows (and it does not claim this must happen; a sphere is convex everywhere). (C) is the only TRUE option.

answer.value: **May be concave in some places and convex in others** — option (C)

optionAnalysis.reason: Every closed object is convex at least at its outermost point, so it cannot be concave everywhere.
A smooth peanut or doughnut has concave regions — convexity everywhere is not required.
Possible (peanut shape) and stated only as a possibility, so it is TRUE.
An edge is itself a non-smooth feature; a smooth surface has neither edges nor corners.

pitfalls: Reading "may" in (C) as "must" — a sphere being convex everywhere does not make (C) false.
Thinking a smooth surface can have edges as long as it has no sharp corners.
cse-2023-ga-5.verification: Sphere: convex everywhere, no edges → refutes (A), consistent with (C). Peanut: smooth with a concave waist → refutes (B), realises (C).

cse-2023-ga-6.approach: Find the assumption the government's action **depends on**: rewarding cycling only addresses "lack of physical exercise" if the government regards cycling as exercise. Everything else goes beyond the passage.

steps.title: Link the problem to the measure
steps.body: Problem stated: lack of physical exercise is a leading cause of the health issues. Measure: money for those who **ride bicycles to work**, taken "to address the problem". The measure can only address *that* problem if cycling counts as physical exercise.

steps.title: That link is what (D) states
steps.body: So the government must **believe** that riding bicycles is a form of physical exercise. (D) is about the government's belief, which the passage's logic guarantees — it does not even need cycling to actually work.

steps.title: Reject statements that go beyond the passage
steps.body:
- (A) An incentive is not a compulsion; nothing says *all* workers will cycle.
- (B) "Ensure **all** … free of health issues" overclaims: lack of exercise is only *one* of the causes.
- (C) The experts only concluded a cause; no suggestion to the government — let alone a mandate — is mentioned (the government chose incentives).

answer.value: **The Government believes riding bicycles is a form of physical exercise** — option (D)

optionAnalysis.reason: Incentives encourage; they do not guarantee that every worker will cycle.
Overclaim: exercise deficit is just one of several leading causes, so cycling cannot ensure everyone is healthy.
The passage never says what the experts recommended; the government chose incentives, not a mandate.
The measure targets lack of exercise, so the government must regard cycling as exercise.

pitfalls: Picking a plausible real-world outcome (A, B) instead of what the text forces.
Confusing the experts' finding (a cause) with a policy recommendation (C).
cse-2023-ga-6.verification: Negation test: if the government did *not* think cycling is exercise, paying people to cycle would not address the stated cause — the passage would make no sense. So (D) is necessary.

cse-2023-ga-7.approach: Study the sign of the difference $g(t) - f(t) = t(4 - 0.01t)$: it changes sign exactly once, at $t = 400$. That one crossing settles both statements.

steps.title: Factor the difference
steps.body:
$$g(t) - f(t) = 4t - 0.01t^2 = t\,(4 - 0.01t)$$
For $t > 0$ the first factor is positive, so the sign is the sign of $4 - 0.01t$, which is zero at $t = \frac{4}{0.01} = 400$.

scene.caption: The curves cross once, at t = 400

steps.title: Statement (ii): $f > g$ for all $t > T$
steps.body: For $t > 400$, $4 - 0.01t < 0$ so $f(t) > g(t)$, for **every** such $t$. Take $T = 400$. Example $t = 500$: $f = 0.01 \times 500^2 = 2500 > g = 2000$. **(ii) is correct.**

intervals.label: f > g for all t > T

optionAnalysis.reason: Misses that the quadratic eventually overtakes the linear function (for $t > 400$).
Misses that for small $t$ (e.g. $t = 1$: $4 > 0.01$) the linear function is larger.
$g > f$ on $(0, 400)$ and $f > g$ for all $t > 400$.
Both statements are verified with explicit values.

cse-2023-ga-7.shortcut: Any $at^2$ with $a > 0$ eventually beats any $bt$, and near $0$ the linear term dominates — so both statements hold without computing the crossing point.
pitfalls: Thinking the small coefficient $0.01$ keeps $f$ below $g$ forever — it only delays the crossing to $t = 400$.
cse-2023-ga-7.verification: At $t = 400$: $f = 0.01 \times 160000 = 1600$ and $g = 4 \times 400 = 1600$ — equal, confirming the single crossing.

cse-2023-ga-8.approach: Use reference words: only one sentence names the character (Mina), so it opens; "the man" must be introduced before "He"; and the stairs must be climbed before she is "on the terrace".

steps.title: Find the opener
steps.body: (i), (ii) and (iv) use pronouns (*she*, *she*, *he*) that need an earlier noun. Only **(iii)** introduces the character by name — *Mina* — and sets the scene (heavy bags). So (iii) comes first.

steps.title: Follow the cause and the movement
steps.body: Heavy bags (iii) explain why **she begins to pant** after climbing all the stairs (ii). Having climbed, she is **"once on the terrace"** (i). So (iii) → (ii) → (i).

steps.title: Place the man
steps.body: (i) introduces **"the man"**; (iv) describes him with **He** — leaning on the parapet, watching the traffic. (iv) must follow (i). Order: **(iii), (ii), (i), (iv)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: Starts with "she" before Mina is introduced and ends with the heavy bags, after she has already reached the terrace.
Panting from the stairs (ii) is placed before the reason for it (iii), and opens with an unexplained "she".
"He" in (iv) opens the passage before the man has been mentioned.
Name → effort on the stairs → arrival on the terrace → the man she notices.

pitfalls: Ignoring pronoun references — a sentence with only "he/she" cannot open a narrative.
cse-2023-ga-8.verification: Read it straight through: "Mina has bought … bags are heavy. She begins to pant … Once on the terrace … she notices the man … He was leaning against the parapet …" — every pronoun has an antecedent and events are in time order.

cse-2023-ga-9.approach: Fix one variable. Holding $y = y_0$ makes $f(x) = g(y_0)$ for **every** $x$, so $f$ is constant; by symmetry $g$ is the same constant. Then test the options against a non-zero constant.

steps.title: Freeze $y$
steps.body: Pick any fixed $y_0$. The condition holds for all $x$, so $f(x) = g(y_0)$ for every real $x$. The right side is a single number, call it $c$: **$f(x) = c$ for all $x$**.

steps.title: Freeze $x$
steps.body: Likewise pick any $x_0$: $g(y) = f(x_0) = c$ for every $y$. Hence **$f(x) = g(y) = c$**, a constant — option (B).

steps.title: Test the other options
steps.body:
Take $f(x) = g(y) = 5$, which satisfies $f(x) = g(y)$ everywhere.
- (A) needs $c = 0$ — false for $c = 5$, so not *necessarily* true.
- (C) contradicts what we proved.
- (D) $f + g = f - g \Rightarrow 2g(y) = 0 \Rightarrow g(y) = 0$; with $c = 5$: $5 + 5 = 10 \ne 0 = 5 - 5$. Not necessary.

optionAnalysis.reason: Zero is one possible constant, not a necessary one: $f = g = 5$ also works.
Fixing either variable shows both functions equal the same constant.
The opposite of what the condition forces.
Simplifies to $g(y) = 0$, which fails for $f = g = 5$.

cse-2023-ga-9.shortcut: A function of $x$ alone can equal a function of $y$ alone for all $x, y$ only if both are the same constant (the standard separation-of-variables argument).
pitfalls: Choosing (A) because $0 = 0$ satisfies the condition — "necessarily" demands it hold in **every** valid case.
cse-2023-ga-9.verification: If $f(x_1) \ne f(x_2)$, then $g(y_0)$ would equal two different numbers — impossible. So $f$ is constant, and so is $g$.

cse-2023-ga-10.approach: Track one distinctive feature — the single **long arm** of the star — plus one short arm as a check. Rotations turn the arm's direction around the clock; a reflection in a horizontal line flips up ↔ down and keeps left/right.
cse-2023-ga-10.given: Long arm of the star: **P** → points up-right; **Q** → points down-right; **R** → points up-right (other arms mirrored compared with P).

steps.title: Operation 1: up-right → down-right
steps.body:
The long arm moves from **up-right** (about 1–2 o'clock) in P to **down-right** (about 4–5 o'clock) in Q: a quarter turn **clockwise**, $90^\circ$.
Check with a short arm: P's arm pointing **straight up** becomes Q's arm pointing **right** — again $90^\circ$ clockwise. A counter-clockwise $90^\circ$ turn would send the long arm up-left; a $180°$ turn would send it down-left.

steps.title: Operation 2: down-right → up-right
steps.body:
From Q to R the long arm goes **down-right → up-right**: left/right is kept, up/down is swapped. That is a **reflection in a horizontal line**.
Check: Q's arm pointing right stays pointing right in R, and Q's arm pointing up becomes R's arm pointing down. A reflection in a vertical line would have sent the long arm to the down-**left**.

steps.title: Match the option
steps.body: Operation 1 = clockwise rotation by $90^\circ$; Operation 2 = reflection along a horizontal line → option **(A)**.

answer.value: **Clockwise 90° rotation, then reflection in a horizontal line** — option (A)

optionAnalysis.reason: Long arm: up-right → (90° clockwise) → down-right → (horizontal mirror) → up-right, matching Q and R.
A 90° counter-clockwise turn would point the long arm up-left, not down-right as in Q.
Operation 1 is right, but a vertical-line reflection of Q would point the long arm down-left, unlike R.
A 180° rotation of P points the long arm down-left, so it cannot give Q.

cse-2023-ga-10.shortcut: Only the long arm matters: NE → SE is 90° clockwise (only A and C), and SE → NE keeps the arm on the right side, so the mirror line is horizontal (A).
pitfalls: Confusing "reflection along a horizontal line" (flips top ↔ bottom) with a vertical line (flips left ↔ right).
Judging the rotation from the overall outline instead of one tracked arm.
cse-2023-ga-10.verification: Compose on a second arm: P's bottom-left arm → 90° clockwise → Q's top-left arm → horizontal mirror → R's bottom-left arm, exactly where R has an arm.

cse-2023-cs-1.approach: Recall the split: the **front-end** (analysis up to intermediate code) depends on the source language but not on the machine; the **back-end** (code generation from the IR) depends on the target machine but not on the source language. Check each statement against that.

steps.title: S1: the front-end is machine-independent
steps.body: The front-end — lexical, syntax and semantic analysis and intermediate-code generation — only reads and checks the **source program** and produces a machine-neutral intermediate representation (IR). None of these phases need to know the target CPU. **S1 is TRUE.**

steps.title: S2: the back-end is target-specific
steps.body: The back-end turns the IR into machine code: instruction selection, register allocation, instruction scheduling, machine-dependent optimisation. These depend on the **instruction set, registers and pipeline** of the target. **S2 is TRUE.**

steps.title: S3: the back-end is NOT language-specific
steps.body: Language-specific work (tokens, grammar, type rules) is all done in the front-end. The back-end sees only the IR, so it is independent of the source language — that is exactly why one back-end can serve many languages (e.g. LLVM serves C, C++, Rust, Swift) and one front-end can target many machines. **S3 is FALSE.**

steps.title: Pick the option
steps.body: S1 true, S2 true, S3 false → **Only S1 and S2 are TRUE** — option (B).

answer.value: **Only S1 and S2 are TRUE** — option (B)

optionAnalysis.reason: Rejects S2, but code generation and register allocation are inherently target-specific.
Front-end: source-language-specific, machine-independent; back-end: machine-specific, language-independent.
Accepts S3, but language-specific phases live in the front-end; the back-end works on the IR only.
Swaps the roles: it accepts S3 (false) and rejects S2 (true).

cse-2023-cs-1.shortcut: Front-end ↔ source language; back-end ↔ target machine. S3 pairs the back-end with the source language, so it is the odd one out.
pitfalls: Mixing up the two dependencies: the front-end is the language-dependent part, the back-end the machine-dependent part.
cse-2023-cs-1.verification: Retargeting argument: with $m$ languages and $n$ machines, a shared IR needs only $m$ front-ends + $n$ back-ends instead of $m \times n$ compilers — possible only if back-ends ignore the source language (S3 false) and front-ends ignore the machine (S1 true).

cse-2023-cs-2.approach: Use the array-heap rule: the children of $A[i]$ are $A[2i]$ and $A[2i+1]$. With $n = 10$, only $i = 1, \dots, 5$ have children, so each option needs at most 9 parent–child comparisons; reject an option at its first violation.

steps.body:
Max-heap: $A[i] \ge A[2i]$ and $A[i] \ge A[2i+1]$ for every $i$ with children. For $n = 10$: parents are $i = 1..\lfloor 10/2 \rfloor = 1..5$, and $A[5]$ has only the child $A[10]$.

| parent | children |
|---|---|
| $A[1]$ | $A[2], A[3]$ |
| $A[2]$ | $A[4], A[5]$ |
| $A[3]$ | $A[6], A[7]$ |
| $A[4]$ | $A[8], A[9]$ |
| $A[5]$ | $A[10]$ |

cse-2023-cs-3.approach: Deleting node `x` means making its **predecessor** point past it. A doubly-linked node stores its predecessor (`x->prev`), so that is $O(1)$; a singly-linked node does not, so `SLLdel` must walk from the head — $O(n)$ in the worst case (when `x` is the last node).

steps.title: What a deletion must change
steps.body: To unlink `x`, the node **before** it must get `pred->next = x->next` (and in a doubly-linked list also `x->next->prev = pred`). If `x` is the head, `head = x->next` instead. So the real question is: **how fast can we reach the predecessor?**

steps.title: SLLdel must search for the predecessor
steps.body: A singly-linked node has only `next`. Starting at `head`, advance `p` until `p->next == x`. In the worst case `x` is the **last** node, so `p` moves $n - 2$ times and makes $n - 1$ comparisons: $\Theta(n)$.

steps.title: The "copy the next node" trick does not save SLLdel
steps.body: For a non-last node one can copy `x->next`'s data into `x` and delete `x->next` in $O(1)$. But the **last** node has no successor to copy from, so it still needs the $O(n)$ walk — and worst-case complexity is decided by that case. **SLLdel is $O(n)$.**

steps.title: DLLdel reaches the predecessor directly

scene.caption: Doubly linked: x->prev gives the predecessor in one step

optionAnalysis.reason: Reversed: it is the singly-linked list that lacks a back pointer and needs the linear search.
Neither list supports a halving search; there is no $\log n$ structure here.
True for `DLLdel` only; `SLLdel` must find the predecessor, $O(n)$ when `x` is the tail.
SLL: walk to the predecessor, $\Theta(n)$ worst case; DLL: use `x->prev`, constant work.

cse-2023-cs-3.shortcut: Deletion cost = cost of finding the predecessor. SLL: search from head → O(n). DLL: `prev` pointer → O(1).
pitfalls: Quoting the copy-next-node trick as O(1) for singly-linked lists — it fails for the last node.
Forgetting that a pointer to the node is given, so DLL deletion needs no search at all.
cse-2023-cs-3.verification: Count operations when `x` is the tail of an $n$-node list: SLL needs $n-1$ `next` comparisons (grows with $n$); DLL needs 2 pointer writes regardless of $n$.
